opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think o1 is a really nice illustration of something we'd been thinking about at Epoch for a while: you can trade compute spent during training against compute spent at inference time. If you have a fixed performance target, you can get there with a bigger, more expensively trained model, or with a smaller model that spends more compute per query, by thinking longer, generating many candidate answers and picking the best, or running chains of reasoning and checking its work.

When we looked at this before o1, across things like Monte Carlo tree search in game-playing, chain-of-thought prompting, and repeated sampling with verifiers, we found that for many of these techniques you could get the equivalent of maybe one to two orders of magnitude of extra training compute by scaling up inference. And the exchange rate was often pretty favorable: spending a bit more at inference could save a lot at training time, at least over some range.

What o1 adds is that the model has been trained specifically to use that inference compute well. Earlier, inference-time techniques were bolted on: you prompt the model to think step by step and hope it helps. With o1, reinforcement learning teaches the model to produce long reasoning traces that actually improve its answers. So the returns to inference compute look much smoother and more reliable, and you get this second scaling curve where performance keeps going up as you let it think longer.

I think there are a few important implications. First, it changes the economics of deployment. If capabilities depend partly on inference spend, then the frontier isn't just set by who has the biggest training run but by who can afford to run models for a long time on hard problems. For really valuable tasks, like research or difficult engineering, you might be willing to spend a lot per query.

Second, it complicates governance approaches based on training compute thresholds. If a model trained at some compute level can perform as if it were trained with ten or a hundred times more compute, just by letting it reason longer, then training compute alone becomes a less complete proxy for what a system can do.

Third, and maybe most interesting, there's a feedback loop: inference compute can generate better reasoning traces and better data, which you can then use to train the next model. So the two aren't really separate budgets. Inference can be turned back into training signal, which is part of why I think this paradigm could sustain fast progress even if we start running into limits on human-generated data.

That said, the trade-off isn't unlimited. Returns to inference scaling tend to diminish, and the curves eventually flatten for a given base model. You can't take a tiny model and make it brilliant just by letting it think forever. So I'd see it as complementary: training compute sets the ceiling, and inference compute determines how close you get to it on a given problem, and both will likely keep scaling together.

r001.rationale: It says that, for a fixed performance target, a smaller model can use more inference compute to match a larger, more expensively trained model.

r002.rationale: It attributes the one-to-two-orders-of-magnitude inference scaling result to Epoch, but does not identify it as a 2022 prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that this trade-off isn't actually new. We've known for a while that you can substitute inference compute for training compute, at least to some degree. If you look at work on things like best-of-n sampling, majority voting, Monte Carlo tree search in games like Go, or even just chain-of-thought prompting, these are all cases where you spend more compute at inference time and get performance that you'd otherwise have needed a bigger or better-trained model to achieve. So the basic phenomenon is familiar.

What o1 does, I think, is show that this substitution can be pushed much further than people expected, and in a fairly general way. The key thing is that they've trained the model to use its inference compute productively, to reason, to check its work, to backtrack when something isn't working, rather than just sampling many times and picking the best answer. And the scaling curves they showed, where performance improves roughly log-linearly in the amount of test-time compute, look quite similar in shape to the training compute scaling curves we're used to. That's a pretty important result if it holds up across domains.

Now, how should we think about the trade-off itself? I find it useful to think of it in terms of what you're actually buying. Training compute is a fixed cost that you pay once, and then it gets amortized over every query the model ever serves. Inference compute is a marginal cost that you pay per query. So if you have a model that's going to be used billions of times, it often makes economic sense to spend a lot upfront on training so that each individual query is cheap. But if you have tasks where the value of getting the right answer is very high, say hard math problems, or scientific questions, or tasks where you'd otherwise need an expensive human expert, then it can make sense to spend a lot more at inference time on those specific tasks.

So I don't think of this as inference compute replacing training compute. I think of it more as opening up a second dimension along which you can scale. And in practice I expect labs will do both. You'll have large training runs, and then on top of that you'll have the ability to dial up inference compute for the queries where it matters.

There are a couple of implications I think are worth drawing out. One is on the economics and the hardware side. If a meaningful fraction of the frontier capability comes from inference-time scaling, then the demand for inference compute goes up a lot, and the total compute spent over a model's lifetime becomes much more weighted toward inference. That changes what kind of chips you want, what kind of data centers you want, and it probably reduces somewhat the advantage of whoever can do the single largest training run, because capabilities become more about total compute budget rather than one giant upfront bet.

The second implication is about how we should forecast capabilities. People have been looking at training compute as the main input and extrapolating from that. If there's now this second lever, then for tasks where test-time compute scales well, you can get capabilities earlier than the training compute trends alone would suggest, just by being willing to spend more per query. And that matters for things like estimating when models will be able to do serious research-level work, where you'd happily spend thousands of dollars of compute on a single hard problem if it meant getting a correct answer.

The last thing I'd flag is that there are limits. The substitution isn't free and it's probably not unbounded. The improvements are log-linear, so each doubling of inference compute buys you a constant increment, which means you can't get arbitrarily far by just spending more at test time. And it seems to work much better in domains where you have some way of verifying answers, like math and coding, than in domains where correctness is fuzzy. So I'd be cautious about assuming this generalizes equally well everywhere. But as a demonstration that the frontier can be pushed on a second axis, I think it's quite significant.

r001.rationale: The response says more inference compute can achieve performance that would otherwise require a bigger or better-trained model, describing inference compute as a substitute for training compute.

r002.rationale: The response discusses inference-time scaling but does not identify Epoch’s 2022 prediction or its estimate of gains equivalent to a tenfold to hundredfold increase in training compute.

astra-6.text:
I think o1 highlights that there are two different places where you can spend compute to improve a model’s performance. You can spend it during training, which gives you a more capable model that you then use across many tasks. Or you can spend it at inference time, giving the model more computation to work through a particular problem before producing an answer.

The economic trade-off is that training is an upfront investment, whereas inference is a cost you incur each time you use the model. If you’re serving a huge number of requests, investing more in training can be attractive because you spread that cost across all those requests. But if you’re solving a particularly valuable, difficult problem, it might make sense to spend substantially more compute on that individual answer.

And these aren’t entirely substitutes. You need training that enables the model to use additional inference compute productively. Simply letting a model generate more text doesn’t necessarily make its answer better. What’s interesting about o1 is the prospect of training models to make better use of that extra computation.

So I’d see this as adding another dimension to scaling. The question becomes not just how large a training run should be, but how to allocate compute between training and answering questions, given the difficulty of the task, the value of a correct answer, and how long you’re willing to wait.

r001.rationale: The response describes training and inference compute as two ways to improve performance, but does not say that more inference compute can make up for less training compute while preserving performance.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Epoch’s 2022 prediction or the tenfold-to-hundredfold comparison.

sol-6.1.text:
I think o1 highlights that there are two ways to spend compute to improve a model’s performance. You can spend more during training to produce a more capable model, or you can spend more at inference time, giving the model more computation to work through a particular problem before answering.

Those investments have different economics. Training is an upfront cost that you spread over all the times the model is used. Inference is a cost you pay each time. So if you’re serving a huge number of queries, investing more in training can be attractive. If you’re solving a small number of very valuable problems, spending substantially more compute on each problem might make sense.

But I wouldn’t view these as straightforward substitutes. Part of what’s interesting about o1 is that training can teach a model to use additional inference compute productively. You need that capability for thinking longer to translate into better answers. So the question becomes: how do you allocate compute between training a system to reason effectively and letting it exercise that ability on the problems you care about? That allocation will depend on both the task and how often you expect to use the system.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts training and inference compute, but explicitly says they are not straightforward substitutes and does not state that more inference compute can preserve performance with less training compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Epoch’s 2022 prediction or the stated tenfold-to-hundredfold equivalence.
